title: Two rice ships and one berth
body:
Shahbandar, the quay office has yesterday's tallies. Whatever was landed, the granary keepers say the town eats faster in the trading season, with every ship's crew ashore to feed.

Expected in port: a junk from Pegu with rice and ship timber; a Javanese junk from Gresik with rice and salt fish; and two Kling ships from the Coromandel coast with cloth. A pepper perahu from Kampar is due on the afternoon tide.

Tides: the Gresik junk must sail by noon to keep company with her fleet. The Pegu captain will wait, but not for nothing: he asks for a promise of the first berth.

Market: rice is dear in the stalls and the poor quarters are grumbling. Timber is wanted at the shipwrights' yards. Cloth is plentiful.

Warning: two rice ships on one morning tide means one of them waits. Decide now whose word you give.

choices.label: Promise the Pegu captain the first berth
choices.outcome_text: The Pegu captain bows and stays. His rice and timber are sure, but the Gresik nakhoda hears of it and says Javanese ships are always kept waiting.

choices.label: Keep the berth for the Gresik junk
choices.outcome_text: You send word that the Gresik junk berths first. The Pegu captain takes it calmly, but he will want something for the delay next time.

choices.label: Promise no one; take ships as the tide brings them
choices.outcome_text: No promise leaves your office. Both captains go back to their ships unsure of their place, and the Pegu captain talks of trying Pasai instead.

notes: The player is a shahbandar; port-wide berthing and inspection authority is a game abstraction; customs rulings are made in the temenggung's name.

Monsoon timing follows docs/research/commodities.md (Pires 1944; Meilink-Roelofsz 1962): western ships arrive on the southwest monsoon (about May to September), Javanese rice on the east winds, China junks sail home on the southwest winds.
Rice suppliers (Pegu, Java) and timber from Pegu: docs/research/commodities.md sections 2 and 3. Foodstuffs paid presents rather than full dues (Pires 1944), so rice choices move supply, not duty.
Ships, people and incidents are fictional. Tide times are game schedule times, not tidal data.
